summary.text:
A clean read that reconciles on three paths — CFR £249.881m rebuilt from Table 2 to the pound, less total debt £176.091m, giving the £73.790m under-borrowing they state themselves.

The whole external book is short-dated. £50m of new loans in the year, every one of them a year or less, including one £5m that ran for two weeks at 7.00%; £55m repaid. Against that sit 34 PWLB loans we hold, £123.0m at 3.246%, of which 32 price below par today — about £26.6m of discount, with £13.0m of it in five loans maturing 2060 to 2064 at 2.45%–2.47%.

The oddity is the property fund. £25.000m of borrowing now nets 1.62% while the fund it supports returns 1.63% net of costs. The two almost exactly cancel.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report and outturn prudential indicators that went to Audit Committee on 13 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We rebuilt your Table 2 from its own components — £246.762m opening, plus £10.684m financed by borrowing, plus £1.138m of right-of-use assets, less £1.500m of JV repayments and £7.203m of MRP and VRP — and it lands on £249.881m exactly. Take off total debt of £176.091m and you get the £73.790m of under-borrowing you state at paragraph 20. Three paths, all to the pound. We also hold 34 PWLB loans for Darlington, £123.0m at a weighted 3.246%, which sits inside the £142.597m of fixed rate debt in your Table 3.

Table 6 is what we wanted to write about. £50m of new loans in the year and every single one a year or less — one of them £5m for two weeks at 7.00%, and the cheapest new money at 3.89% and 3.93% on one-year terms. £55m repaid against it. Running an entire external programme on short-dated market and local authority money is a real strategy and paragraphs 33 to 36 set out the reasoning plainly, including the sentence about avoiding higher costs later "when this authority may not be able to avoid new borrowing". We have no view on whether that is right.

What we can add is the other side of the same market, which no single council can see from its own papers. Nobody publishes what everyone else is paying for short-dated inter-authority money, so whether 7.00% for a fortnight was the going rate that week or an outlier is not answerable from inside one treasury. We track it across the sector, alongside the PWLB side: July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is a thin month. Both are at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Second, the long half of your book, which the short-term activity rather hides. Thirty-two of your thirty-four PWLB loans price below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, notice 314/26 — about £26.6m of discount in total against a £123.0m balance. Five loans maturing between 2060 and 2064 at 2.45% to 2.47% carry roughly £13.0m of that between them, and the two £4.6m annuities at 1.65% running to 2070 another £4.3m. We are not suggesting anything follows: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. The point is narrower — that a book which looks quiet in the annual report is moving underneath, and it is easier to watch daily than to reconstruct once a year. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The third thing is the property fund, and we raise it only because the two numbers sit one line apart in your own tables and are easy to miss. £25.000m of borrowing supporting the position now nets 1.62%, while the fund returns 1.63% net of costs. They almost exactly cancel. Table 7 shows the gross return at 4.12% against 3.74% budgeted, so the gap is costs rather than performance. With Lothbury wound up and Hermes Federated having returned £8.896m in cash which went to repay maturing debt, the shape of that position has changed a good deal in one year.

On training, four fit Darlington. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and Liquidity & cashflow forecasting go to Table 6 and a book that reprices continuously. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator covers the discount position. And Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) for the property fund side. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
